clue.text: Utmost strength in the constituents of sea-power

definitions.meaning: full force, as in striving with every ounce
the main is the open ocean and might is power, the two parts of sea-power

explanation.surface: A naval essay on what makes a country's strength at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase means all one's force; split up, 'might' is power and 'main' is the sea, so sea-power is made of the two.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'with all one's force' covers utmost strength, and its two nouns are a word for power and an old word for the ocean.

clue.text: One in the eye for Wooster ?

definitions.text: One in the eye for Wooster ?

parts.words: One in the eye for Wooster
parts.note: 'one in the eye' reads as a snub, but here it is a single lens worn in one eye by a P. G. Wodehouse toff

explanation.surface: A setback for a Wodehouse hero.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One in the eye' is an idiom for a rebuff; read literally it is a single glass in one eye, the eyeglass of the stage silly-ass Englishman such as Bertie Wooster.
explanation.definitionFit: A single eyeglass held in one eye socket is exactly one lens in one eye.

clue.text: Carrying a little weight, Manx cat puffs a lot

definitions.note: the definition stands for 'one who puffs a lot', a heavy breather

parts.note: a gram is a small unit of weight

indicators.note: a Manx cat has no tail, so the word for cat loses its last letter

explanation.surface: A fat tailless cat from the Isle of Man wheezing about.
explanation.walkthrough: Manx cats are born without tails, so PUSS is docked to PUS; 'Carrying' just joins the weight to the cat.
explanation.definitionFit: Besides the whale, the word is used for a person who breathes noisily and heavily, as the blowing whale does.

clue.text: They're charming-one of them was Scott's

definitions.meaning: charms or amulets, objects thought to work magic
Sir Walter Scott's novel 'The Talisman' takes its title from such an amulet

explanation.surface: Charms praised, one of them owned by a famous writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Walter Scott wrote the novel 'The Talisman', so one such object was his.
explanation.definitionFit: Amulets are things that charm, in the old magical sense, and Scott's crusading novel is named after one of them.

clue.text: Tell-tales from the ranks

indicators.note: the answer is made from the letters of the next word, reshaped

explanation.surface: Informers drawn from among the common soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' tells you the answer is made out of the letters of RANKS rearranged; British slang 'nark' means a police informer.
explanation.definitionFit: A nark is slang for an informer, someone who tells on others.

clue.text: An angelic leader:

parts.note: the archangel who leads the heavenly host against Satan

explanation.surface: Someone who heads a band of angels.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Bible and Milton the archangel commands the armies of heaven, so he is literally a leader of angels.
explanation.definitionFit: The archangel named in Revelation leads the angelic host in war against the dragon.

clue.text: It's a bit thick, a painter might say

definitions.text: It's a bit thick, a painter might say

parts.words: It's a bit thick, a painter might say
parts.note: 'a bit thick' means 'unfair', but here it is paint laid on in thick layers

explanation.surface: An artist complaining that something is unreasonable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's a bit thick' is British slang for 'that's too much'; the painter means literally thick paint on the canvas.
explanation.definitionFit: The term names paint applied so heavily that brush or knife marks stand up from the canvas.

clue.text: PS. This is no murderous malice

definitions.meaning: a postscript, something added after a letter is finished
murder needs malice aforethought, planned beforehand; an idea arriving late is the opposite

explanation.surface: A postscript that turns out to be about murder.
explanation.walkthrough: In law 'malice aforethought' is the planned intent behind murder; swap 'afore' for 'after' and it is no longer murderous.
explanation.definitionFit: A postscript is something added later, an idea that comes late; and it is the opposite of the premeditation that defines murder.

clue.text: Only its non-arrival would put the breeze up a film star

definitions.text: Only its non-arrival would put the breeze up a film star

parts.words: Only its non-arrival would put the breeze up a film star
parts.note: 'put the breeze up' means frighten; a star is scared only when admirers' letters stop coming, and admirers are fans, which also make a breeze

explanation.surface: A film star is scared only when something fails to turn up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put the breeze up' is British slang for alarm; it also hints at a fan blowing air, and fans are admirers who write to stars.
explanation.definitionFit: Letters from admirers pour in for a star, so their drying up is a sign of fading fame.

clue.text: Instructions to prepare items for board meetings ?

definitions.text: Instructions to prepare items for board meetings ?

parts.words: Instructions to prepare items for board meetings
parts.note: 'board' here is the table at which meals are served, not a company board, so the items are dishes

explanation.surface: Briefing papers for directors before a company meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Board' as in 'bed and board' means food at table, so the meetings are meals and the items are dishes.
explanation.definitionFit: Cooking directions tell you how to make dishes for the table.

clue.text: A bit of a farm rather than a baby-farm

definitions.text: A bit of a farm rather than a baby-farm

parts.words: A bit of a farm rather than a baby-farm
parts.note: split the answer as 'small' plus 'holding': a little plot of land, not a place where little ones are held

explanation.surface: A small plot of farmland, as opposed to a nursery for infants.
explanation.walkthrough: A baby-farm was a place taking in infants for pay, which would be 'holding the small'; the answer is a modest plot of farmland.
explanation.definitionFit: A plot of agricultural land smaller than a farm is a little piece of farming country.

clue.text: Successful results of free enterprise?

parts.note: 'free enterprise' reads as capitalism, but here it is an attempt to get free, as by a prisoner

explanation.surface: An economist praising the fruits of capitalism.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Free enterprise' looks like economics; read as an enterprise to get free, its successes are breakouts.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting away from captivity is what a successful bid for freedom achieves.

clue.text: As new as can be in the Principality

definitions.note: the definition stands for 'a place in the Principality', a town in Wales

indicators.note: the letters of the preceding words could be turned into the answer if rearranged

explanation.surface: Something as fresh as anything you could find in Wales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can be' signals that the letters of AS NEW AS can be rearranged; 'the Principality' is Wales, a principality of the UK.
explanation.definitionFit: This port city lies on the south coast of Wales, which is often called the Principality.

clue.text: Stretchers to boot

parts.note: 'to boot' seems to mean 'as well', but these stretchers go into a boot to keep its shape

explanation.surface: Stretchers thrown in as an extra.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To boot' means 'in addition'; read literally, these are shaped blocks put inside a boot to stretch it.
explanation.definitionFit: Wooden shoe or boot forms are put inside footwear to stretch and keep its shape.

clue.text: An Anglophobe might have considered Browning one

definitions.text: An Anglophobe might have considered Browning one

parts.words: An Anglophobe might have considered Browning one
parts.note: Robert Browning wrote 'Oh, to be in England now that April's there'; someone who hates England would think him a fool for that wish

explanation.surface: A hater of the English dismissing a Victorian poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Browning's 'Home-Thoughts, from Abroad' longs for England in April, so an England-hater would think him a fool about April.
explanation.definitionFit: A dupe of 1 April pranks is a fool tied to that month, as Browning was in his longing for an English spring.

clue.text: Removed the stopper, perhaps ?

parts.note: 'stopper' seems to be a cork, but it is whatever stopped things; once it is removed, things got going again

explanation.surface: Someone uncorking a bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stopper' suggests a bottle cork; read as whatever halted progress, taking it away means things began again.
explanation.definitionFit: Began again after a halt, which is what follows clearing an obstacle that had stopped things.

clue.text: They hoped to follow the company in a concert party

definitions.text: They hoped to follow the company in a concert party

parts.words: They hoped to follow the company in a concert party
parts.note: hopeful people; and a famous 1920s British concert party put such people after CO, the abbreviation for company, in its name

explanation.surface: Hopeful performers wishing to join a touring troupe.
explanation.walkthrough: The Co-Optimists were a famous British concert party (a variety troupe) of the 1920s: in its name the hopeful ones come after CO, short for company.
explanation.definitionFit: People who look on the bright side are those who hope for the best.

clue.text: Trainer changes the ground

indicators.note: the letters of the word before it are altered into a new order

explanation.surface: A racehorse trainer switching courses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changes' signals that the letters of TRAINER are rearranged; a trainer changing ground suits horse racing.
explanation.definitionFit: The lie of the land is the stretch of country underfoot.

clue.text: They had their attractions, Bob Cherry, Bunter & Co

definitions.meaning: objects that pull iron towards them
Frank Richards's Greyfriars schoolboys appeared weekly in 'The Magnet'

explanation.surface: Schoolboy characters admired for their appeal.
explanation.walkthrough: Billy Bunter and Bob Cherry of Greyfriars School first appeared in 'The Magnet', a British boys' weekly paper.
explanation.definitionFit: Lodestones draw iron, so they have attraction; and Bunter's stories ran in a boys' paper with that name.

clue.text: Place for courtship in Spain ?

parts.note: 'courtship' seems to mean wooing, but here it is the state of being a court, an open courtyard of a Spanish house

explanation.surface: Where Spanish lovers go courting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Courtship' looks like romance; split as 'court' plus '-ship' it is a courtyard, the Spanish inner yard of a house.
explanation.definitionFit: The paved inner yard of a Spanish house is its open-air court.

clue.text: Kind of hat for a pastry-cook?

definitions.meaning: a flat-crowned felt hat with a turned-up brim
a raised meat pie, something a baker makes

explanation.surface: Headgear suitable for a baker.
explanation.walkthrough: A pork pie hat is a flat-crowned felt hat; a pork pie is a cold British meat pie in a raised pastry case.
explanation.definitionFit: The low flat-topped hat is named for its shape, like a raised meat pie, which a baker would make.

clue.text: Sources of home-brewed?

parts.note: 'home-brewed' suggests beer, but the brew here is a cup of tea made at home

explanation.surface: Where homemade beer comes from.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Home-brewed' points to beer; in British homes the everyday brew is tea, poured from the pot.
explanation.definitionFit: Tea is said to brew in the vessel from which it is poured.

clue.text: Wherein one expects to find gas and gear anyway

definitions.text: Wherein one expects to find gas and gear anyway

indicators.note: the letters of the two words are taken in any old order, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Where you would naturally look for petrol and car parts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anyway' tells you to rearrange GAS and GEAR together; the whole clue is also the definition, as these places hold petrol and car parts.
explanation.definitionFit: Service stations and car workshops stock fuel and motor parts.

clue.text: Best way to make the money, go round

definitions.text: Best way to make the money, go round

parts.words: Best way to make the money, go round
parts.note: 'make the money go round' sounds like stretching a budget, but literally money circulates when you part with it

explanation.surface: Advice on making a budget last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make the money go round' usually means economise; the clue reads it as keeping cash in circulation, which only happens when you pay it out.
explanation.definitionFit: Paying out cash puts it into circulation, passing it to others.

clue.text: An attack by the Flying Squad ?

definitions.text: An attack by the Flying Squad ?

parts.words: An attack by the Flying Squad
parts.note: the Flying Squad is a London police unit that makes raids; read literally, a flying squad attacks from the sky

explanation.surface: A police swoop on criminals.
explanation.walkthrough: The Flying Squad is Scotland Yard's robbery unit; taken literally, a squad that flies makes its raids from the air.
explanation.definitionFit: Bombers attacking from above carry out an assault from the sky.

clue.text: If you're looking for hangers-on, try the bar

definitions.text: If you're looking for hangers-on, try the bar

parts.words: If you're looking for hangers-on, try the bar
parts.note: 'hangers-on' seem to be spongers in a pub, but here they are acrobats hanging from a swinging bar

explanation.surface: Advice that freeloaders gather in the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hangers-on' and 'bar' suggest cadgers at a pub counter; the bar is a circus swing from which acrobats hang.
explanation.definitionFit: A swinging bar hung from ropes is what circus acrobats hang from.

clue.text: A big blow for Conrad:

definitions.meaning: a violent tropical storm with strong wind
Joseph Conrad's 1902 sea story bears this title

explanation.surface: A heavy punch thrown at a novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: Joseph Conrad wrote the novella 'Typhoon' (1902), so the storm was his title.
explanation.definitionFit: A tropical storm is a huge wind, and Conrad named a sea story after one.

clue.text: Partiality for being left alone?

definitions.meaning: 'left alone' read as only one side being left, a state of having a single side

explanation.surface: A preference for solitude.
explanation.walkthrough: Partiality is bias; the second reading takes 'left alone' as being left on one side only.
explanation.definitionFit: Bias favours one party, and something left on one side only has a single side.
